opus-5.5.text:
I think the parallel is actually really striking, and it's one of the framings I find most useful when I explain what we're trying to do.

If you go back to the Human Genome Project, the big milestone was sequencing: getting the full readout of the As, Ts, Cs and Gs. That was a monumental achievement, but it turned out to be the beginning rather than the end. Having the sequence didn't mean we understood what any of it did. We had this enormous string of code that clearly ran the system, and we could barely read it. It took decades more work in functional genomics to figure out which regions encode proteins, which are regulatory, how genes interact, and how a variant in one place leads to a disease somewhere else.

Neural networks are in a very similar position today, maybe even a more extreme one. We have perfect access to every weight and every activation. In a sense, the "sequence" is fully known. But knowing every number in a model with hundreds of billions of parameters tells you almost nothing about why it produced a particular answer, or what concepts it's representing internally. So interpretability is, in a way, the functional genomics of AI. We're trying to go from raw parameters to a mechanistic understanding: these features correspond to these concepts, these circuits implement this behavior, and this is what you'd change to fix a specific failure.

The other part of the analogy I like is where it leads. Once biology could read the genome functionally, you got targeted interventions: diagnostics, gene therapies, eventually editing tools like CRISPR. That's the arc I'd hope for in AI. Today, when a model hallucinates or behaves in a way we don't want, the main tools are pretty blunt. You retrain, you add more data, you do RLHF and hope the behavior goes away without breaking something else. That's a bit like treating a disease without knowing its mechanism. If we can actually understand the internals, we can diagnose why a model does something and make precise edits, almost like surgery on the model's cognition.

There's one place where the analogy breaks down, and it's encouraging. In biology, experiments are slow, expensive, and often ethically constrained. You can't just knock out a gene in a person and see what happens. With neural networks, we can intervene on any neuron or feature, run millions of experiments, and observe the results instantly. So while the challenge is similar in spirit, I think the pace of progress in interpretability can be dramatically faster than it was in genomics. That's a big part of why I'm optimistic we can get to real understanding, and real control, of these systems on a timescale that matters.

r001.rationale: The response presents AI interpretability as analogous to functional genomics and describes applying interpretability to neural networks; it does not identify understanding the human genome as an application of AI interpretability.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the parallel is actually pretty deep, and it's one of the things that drew me to this work in the first place.

When the Human Genome Project finished, there was this feeling that we'd cracked it. We had the sequence. But what we quickly realized was that having the sequence and understanding what it does are completely different problems. Three billion base pairs, and most of what we could say at first was "this region seems to correlate with this trait." It took years of building tools, like understanding gene regulation, epigenetics, and how proteins fold, before we could go from "here's the raw data" to "here's the mechanism."

With neural networks, we're in a very similar place. We have the weights. Every single parameter is right there, we can read them off. But a frontier model has hundreds of billions of these, and the knowledge isn't stored in a way that maps neatly onto human concepts. It's distributed, it's superimposed, you have a single neuron that lights up for a dozen unrelated things. So just like the genome, having complete access to the substrate doesn't give you understanding for free.

What I find encouraging about the analogy is the trajectory. Genomics went from correlation to mechanism by developing the right abstractions, and that's exactly what interpretability is trying to do. Things like dictionary learning or sparse autoencoders are our attempt to find the "genes" of a model, the actual units of meaning that the raw weights are encoding. And circuits work is like going from genes to pathways: how do these features combine to actually produce a behavior?

There are a couple of places the analogy breaks down, though, and I think they're worth being honest about. One is that we built these models. We know the training procedure and the data, so in principle we have a kind of experimental access that biologists never had with evolution. We can run ablations at scale, we can retrain with changes. The other difference cuts the opposite way: the genome is the product of billions of years of selection and it's relatively stable. Models change every few months. So we're trying to build a science of something that keeps mutating under us, which means our tools have to generalize across architectures or they're obsolete the moment they're published.

But the core lesson from genomics that I keep coming back to is that it took a long time and it was worth it. Nobody today would argue we shouldn't have invested in understanding the genome just because the early years were slow. I think we'll look back on interpretability the same way.

r001.rationale: The response presents genome research as an analogy for AI interpretability, but does not identify understanding the human genome as a direct application of AI interpretability.

astra-6.text:
I think the parallel is that having access to the underlying code doesn’t automatically mean we understand how it works. You can read a genome, but that’s very different from understanding how those sequences interact to produce a particular trait. Similarly, we can inspect a model’s weights without being able to explain how they give rise to a particular behavior.

In both cases, you need to move from observation to experiments. If you change something, does the outcome change in the way your explanation predicts? That’s a much stronger test of understanding than finding a correlation.

There are limits to the analogy, of course. But I think it captures why interpretability is hard: we have these relatively simple building blocks, and the behavior emerges from their interactions. Having the whole sequence—or all the weights—is a starting point, not a complete explanation.

r001.rationale: The response describes understanding the genome as an analogy to AI interpretability, but does not identify it as a direct application of AI interpretability.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the parallel is that having access to the underlying code doesn’t mean you understand how the system works. You can read a genome, but that doesn’t immediately tell you how a particular trait emerges. Similarly, you can inspect a model’s weights without understanding how they produce a particular behavior.

In both cases, the challenge is moving from description to causal understanding. Can we identify a component, form a hypothesis about what it does, and then intervene to see whether that hypothesis holds? And how does its role change depending on the other components around it?

The analogy has limits, because we can experiment on AI models in ways we can’t on humans. But I think the shared lesson is that getting the full sequence—or all the weights—is the beginning of the science, not the end.

r001.rationale: The response describes a parallel between AI interpretability and studying the genome, but does not identify understanding the human genome as an application of AI interpretability.
